“I certainly should want his record investigated,” said Mr. Hawthorne. “Why did you ask if he found me, Mr. Burke? Was he looking for me?”

“When he’d eyed me for a minute, queer and uncertain like,” Thomas Burke resumed, “he asked did I know the countryside well? An’ I told him I ought to, drivin’ it constant for upwards of seven years. An’ he asked did I know any one named Hawthorne, Gilbert Hawthorne, an’, says I, I do. Leastways, I know a little about him, nor did I say he was lookin’ after me friend, Poppy, though I might have, I might have!” Mr. Burke smiled into Poppy’s face, thrust forward as she perched on the edge of a chair as if afraid that a word might slip past her.

“Then he asked me, an’ I told him where you lived, sir, an’ he listened tight, an’ he sort of muttered that maybe he’d see you. ‘Maybe I will,’ he said, an’ he shook his head hard. I misdoubted he was right in his mind, but I let him go on—he wouldn’t ride wid me, though I asked him. Ever since it’s been botherin’ me that maybe it was something you ought to know about, an’ more an’ more did it bother me the longer I thought about it, till the missus says: ‘Gwan wid you, Tom, an’ see Mr. Hawthorne. Make it your way to go to Greenacres sooner than you’re due there, an’ see him an’ tell him the little there is to tell, an’ get it off your conscience.’ So I’m here, an’ you’re told, an’ for my part of it, there’s no more about it. You don’t know the man; there’s no mischief afoot, is there?”

“Not that I know of; no, I don’t know any one like the person you describe. Curious, too, especially that he was in the woods near the children’s tree house—if it were the same man,” said Mr. Hawthorne slowly.

“Oh, it was, daddy; it had to be!” cried Mark. “There couldn’t be two like that in one neighborhood. Say, isn’t it great? It sounds like a story with a plot to it.”

text: A maple is a deciduous tree or shrub belonging to the genus Acer, with over 130 species distributed across temperate regions of North America, Europe, and Asia, widely admired for its stunning foliage, distinctive palmate leaves, vibrant autumn colors, and valuable wood and syrup products. Maple trees vary in size from small ornamental shrubs under 3 meters tall to large canopy trees exceeding 40 meters in height, with dense, rounded crowns that provide ample shade during summer. Their most recognizable feature is their palmately lobed leaves, typically with 3 to 9 pointed lobes, which turn brilliant shades of red, orange, yellow, gold, and crimson during autumn before falling, creating spectacular seasonal landscapes. Maple trees produce small, clustered flowers in early spring, followed by distinctive winged seeds called samaras, also known as helicopter seeds, which spin as they fall to disperse efficiently by wind. The bark of mature maple trees is often grayish-brown, textured, and furrowed, providing winter interest after leaves have fallen. Sugar maples, native to eastern North America, are the primary source of maple syrup, a sweet natural product made by tapping tree trunks to collect sap during late winter and early spring, then boiling it down to concentrate the sugars. It takes approximately 40 liters of maple sap to produce just 1 liter of pure maple syrup, making it a valuable and labor-intensive product. Maple wood is hard, dense, and fine-grained, highly valued for furniture making, flooring, cabinetry, musical instruments, cutting boards, and veneer due to its durability, workability, and attractive grain pattern. Ecologically, maples support diverse wildlife, providing buds, flowers, seeds, and shelter for birds, squirrels, insects, and deer, while their root systems stabilize soil and prevent erosion. Many maple species are widely cultivated as ornamental trees in parks, gardens, streets, and urban landscapes for their aesthetic appeal, shade provision, and brilliant fall color display. Popular landscape species include Japanese maple, known for its delicate foliage and striking red or purple leaves, and the Norway maple, a hardy urban-tolerant species. Maples thrive in well-drained, fertile soil with full sunlight to partial shade, adapting well to a range of climatic conditions within temperate zones. They are relatively low-maintenance trees, resistant to many pests and diseases, though susceptible to certain fungal infections and aphid infestations in some regions. Culturally, maple leaves hold significant symbolic value, most notably as the national emblem of Canada, featured prominently on the Canadian flag. Maples also symbolize balance, love, longevity, and abundance in various cultural traditions and art forms. In autumn, maple-dominated forests create some of the most visually stunning seasonal scenery in the world, attracting tourists and nature enthusiasts globally. Maple branches and leaves are commonly used in decorative arrangements, crafts, and seasonal decorations, particularly during autumn festivals. The trees’ rapid growth rate and attractive appearance make them a staple of temperate forest ecosystems and human-designed landscapes alike. Whether valued for syrup production, timber quality, ecological benefits, or ornamental beauty, maples are among the most versatile and beloved trees in temperate regions. Their vibrant seasonal transformation combines ecological function with aesthetic splendor, making them an integral part of natural landscapes and cultural heritage across continents.

At length he stopped before a shop of a rather better description than those he had hitherto passed; and, after looking around him for some time, as if to ascertain that he was not watched, he knocked at the door. A feeble 'Come in' answered the knock, and the stranger, opening the door, entered a small and dimly lighted room. In a chair by a scanty fire sat a man of about the age of fifty, with a countenance on which crime and care had left their traces. He looked up hastily as the stranger entered. 'You are poor, friend,' said the stranger. 'I am,' was the reply. 'And I,' said the stranger, 'am rich. Will you earn this?' and he showed him a piece of gold. The man's eyes sparkled. 'What would you have me do?' 'You are an outcast,' continued the stranger; 'you have neither friends nor character. I offer you wealth.' The man looked suspiciously at the speaker. 'What is the nature of the service?' he asked. 'You shall know in time,' replied the stranger; 'meantime, take this, and meet me here again tomorrow night at the same hour.' So saying, he placed the money in the man's hand, and turned to depart. 'Stay,' said the man; 'you have not even told me your name.' 'My name is of no consequence,' replied the stranger; 'call me what you will.' And without another word, he left the house, and was soon lost in the darkness of the street.

text: The old inn, known by the name of the Admiral Benbow, was a solitary, quiet place, standing on a cliff that overlooked the sea. It was a square, white building, with a faded blue signboard that swung and creaked in the wind. On either side of the door were benches where the customers might sit and look out over the water. The cliff was steep and rocky, covered with short, wiry grass that was almost always wet with sea-spray. Behind the inn, the land rose to a high, dark hill, covered with pine trees that murmured continually. The place had a wild, lonely beauty that appealed to those who loved the sea. My father, who kept the inn, was a quiet man, fond of reading and of his own company. He had chosen this spot because of its solitude, and because it gave him the opportunity to indulge in his favorite pastime of watching the ships that passed along the coast. From the windows of the inn, one could see for miles over the water, and on clear days the white sails of the vessels showed like specks against the blue. The inn itself was furnished in a plain, homely style. The floors were of bare wood, scrubbed white with sand, and the furniture was heavy and old-fashioned. In the tap-room there was a great fireplace, where a fire was always burning, and on the walls were pictures of ships and naval battles. The air was always full of the smell of salt and tar and wood-smoke, a combination that seemed to belong to the place as much as the sound of the waves on the rocks below. The customers were mostly fishermen and coasting sailors, men of few words but honest hearts. They would sit for hours over their ale, talking in low voices of the sea and its dangers, of wrecks and rescues, of strange sights seen in far-off waters. Sometimes, on stormy nights, when the wind howled around the building and the waves thundered against the cliff, the inn seemed like a refuge from the fury of the elements, a warm, bright spot in the midst of the darkness and the storm.

text: The winter night in Watanabe Toru’s dorm room at the University of Tokyo was quiet—quiet enough that the only sounds were the faint crackle of John Coltrane’s record on the turntable and the soft tap of snowflakes against the window. Watanabe sat cross-legged on the floor, his back leaning against the cold wall, a half-empty cup of instant coffee beside him and a tattered copy of The Great Gatsby open on his lap. The room was small and cluttered: a wooden desk piled with lecture notes and cigarette butts, a single bookshelf filled with jazz records and paperbacks, and a faded poster of Miles Davis taped above the bed— a gift from his friend Kizuki, back when they were still in high school. He thought of Naoko—of the way she’d smiled when they walked through the woods together last spring, her hair tied back with a blue ribbon, her hands cold even through her gloves. She’d talked about the stars, about how they felt “far away but still close,” and he’d listened, not saying much, just enjoying the sound of her voice. Now, she was in the sanatorium, miles away, and he hadn’t heard from her in three weeks. He wondered if she was thinking of him, too—if she still remembered the way the sunlight filtered through the trees, or the way they’d shared a single earbud to listen to Coltrane’s My Favorite Things. The record skipped, and Watanabe reached over to adjust the needle, his fingers brushing the worn vinyl. He thought of Midori—of the way she’d burst into his classroom last month, her raincoat dripping wet, holding up a bag of chestnuts and saying “I found these and thought of you.” She was loud, and messy, and nothing like Naoko—nothing like the quiet, fragile girl he’d grown used to. But there was something about her—something in the way she laughed, in the way she didn’t hide her feelings—that made his chest feel light, like he was breathing for the first time in a long while. He closed The Great Gatsby, setting it aside. The coffee had gone cold, but he picked it up anyway, taking a sip. He thought of Kizuki—of the way they’d stayed up all night talking about music and girls, of the way Kizuki’s guitar had sounded in the empty classroom, of the day he’d found Kizuki’s note on his desk, short and simple: “I’m sorry.” That day had broken something in him, something he wasn’t sure he’d ever fix. It had made him realize how fragile life was, how easy it was to lose someone—even someone you thought you’d never be without. A snowflake stuck to the window, melting slowly into a tiny drop of water. Watanabe stood up, walking to the window, and pressed his palm against the glass. Outside, the campus was covered in a thin layer of snow, the streetlights casting soft yellow circles on the ground. He thought of Naoko’s blue ribbon, of Midori’s chestnuts, of Kizuki’s guitar—all the little things that made up his life, all the things he didn’t want to forget. The record ended, and the room fell silent, except for the tap of snowflakes and the distant hum of a passing train. Watanabe stood there for a while, watching the snow fall, his breath fogging the window.

text: Now, you red-eyed devil, he said, when he had made an opening sufficient for the passage of Buck's body. At the same time he dropped the hatchet and shifted the club to his right hand. And Buck was truly a red-eyed devil, as he drew himself together for the spring, hair bristling, mouth foaming, a mad glitter in his blood-shot eyes. Straight at the man he launched his one hundred and forty pounds of fury, surcharged with the pent passion of two days and nights. In mid air, just as his jaws were about to close on the man, he received a shock that checked his body and brought his teeth together with an agonizing clip. He whirled over, fetching the ground on his back and side. He had never been struck by a club in his life, and did not understand. With a snarl that was part bark and more scream he was again on his feet and launched into the air. And again the shock came and he was brought crushingly to the ground. This time he was aware that it was the club, but his madness knew no caution. A dozen times he charged, and as often the club broke the charge and smashed him down. After a particularly fierce blow, he crawled to his feet, too dazed to rush. He staggered limply about, the blood flowing from nose and mouth and ears, his beautiful coat sprayed and flecked with bloody slaver. Then the man advanced and deliberately dealt him a frightful blow on the nose. All the pain he had endured was as nothing compared with the exquisite agony of this. With a roar that was almost lionlike in its ferocity, he again hurled himself at the man. But the man, shifting the club from right to left, coolly caught him by the under jaw, at the same time wrenching downward and backward. Buck described a complete circle in the air, and half of another, then crashed to the ground on his head and chest. For the last time he rushed. The man struck the shrewd blow he had purposely withheld for so long, and Buck crumpled up and went down, knocked utterly senseless. He's no slouch at dog-breakin', that's wot I say, one of the men on the wall cried enthusiastically. Druther break cayuses any day, and twice on Sundays, was the reply of the driver, as he climbed on the wagon and started the horses. Buck's senses came back to him, but not his strength. He lay where he had fallen, and from there he watched the man in the red sweater.

text: The school’s annual Art Festival was only four weeks away, and Ms. Rivera’s class needed to create a big installation for the hallway. “Let’s make a ‘Tree of Dreams’— we’ll cover it with colorful notes of hopes and talents!” Mia suggested. The class cheered, and Ms. Rivera nodded: “But it needs to be teamwork— everyone brings their strengths.” They split into groups. Leo, who loved building, led the structure team. He planned to use cardboard tubes and wooden dowels to make the tree trunk and branches. “We need to make it sturdy enough to hold hundreds of notes,” he said, sketching designs in his notebook. Zoe and her group took charge of color and decoration. They collected old magazines, tissue paper, and paint to cover the trunk with bright patterns. “We’ll add glitter and ribbons— it’ll look like it’s glowing!” Zoe exclaimed, sorting through a pile of craft supplies. Jake’s team was in charge of collecting the dream notes. They made blank cards with prompts like “I hope to ______” and “My talent is ______” and passed them out to every class. “We need to get as many notes as possible— the more, the merrier!” Jake said, taping the cards to a poster board. At first, everything went smoothly. But after a week, Leo’s team hit a problem: the branches kept bending under the weight of the first few test notes. “It’s not strong enough,” he groaned. The class gathered to brainstorm. “What if we add crossbars inside the branches?” Zoe suggested. Jake nodded: “And we can use thicker dowels for the main branches.” Leo’s team adjusted the design, adding extra support and swapping thin dowels for thicker ones. Zoe’s group helped reinforce the branches with colorful tape, turning the fixes into part of the decoration. Jake’s team kept collecting notes, and soon the pile grew taller than their desk. On the weekend before the festival, the whole class came to school to assemble the tree. Leo’s team built the trunk and branches, Zoe’s group wrapped them in vibrant paper and glitter, and Jake’s team taped the dream notes to every branch. They worked together, laughing as they climbed step stools to reach the top branches and passed supplies to each other. By afternoon, the “Tree of Dreams” stood tall in the hallway— its trunk wrapped in rainbow patterns, branches covered in hundreds of colorful notes, and ribbons fluttering in the breeze. Ms. Rivera took a photo, smiling: “This is what teamwork looks like— everyone’s part matters.” On the day of the festival, students and teachers crowded around the tree, reading the notes. “I love how each part fits together,” a teacher said. Leo, Zoe, and Jake high-fived. “We couldn’t have done it alone,” Leo said. Zoe nodded: “When we helped each other, we fixed problems fast.” Jake added: “And the tree turned out better than any of us could have made alone!” That night, Mia wrote a final note and taped it to the top branch: “My dream is to always work together— because we’re stronger as a team.” As she walked away, she smiled, knowing that the best part of the Art Festival wasn’t the tree itself. It was the fun of creating something amazing with her friends.

text: The zebra is a striking, highly recognizable African equid mammal closely related to domestic horses and wild donkeys, world-famous for its unique, bold black-and-white striped coat that makes it one of the most distinctive animals in the entire natural world. Remarkably, every individual zebra possesses a completely unique stripe pattern, much like human fingerprints, with natural variations in stripe width, curvature, density, and pattern across the three main species: plains zebras, mountain zebras, and Grévy’s zebras. Adult zebras generally have a body length ranging from 2 to 2.7 meters, a shoulder height between 1.2 and 1.5 meters, and a strong, muscular build built for endurance running and survival in open grassland habitats. Zebras have long heads with relatively small jaws, short erect manes along the neck, large mobile ears for excellent hearing, and powerful legs capable of reaching running speeds up to 65 kilometers per hour to escape predators such as lions, hyenas, leopards, and wild dogs. Multiple scientific theories suggest potential advantages of the distinctive striped coat, including camouflage within tall grassland vegetation, confusing predators during high-speed chases, deterring biting flies and other parasites, and assisting with thermal regulation through micro-air currents created by the contrasting stripes. Zebras are extremely social herd animals that live in tight-knit family groups or larger herds, which provide increased vigilance and protection against predators; they communicate using a combination of brays, barks, facial expressions, ear positioning, and body language. As obligate grazers, zebras feed primarily on coarse grasses, though they will also browse on leaves, shoots, and tree bark when grass is scarce during dry seasons. Their specialized digestive systems allow them to process low-quality, high-fiber vegetation that many other herbivores cannot digest, enabling survival in arid savanna and grassland ecosystems. Female zebras have a lengthy gestation period of approximately 12 months, typically giving birth to a single foal that is born with brownish-orange and white stripes that gradually darken to black as it matures. Newborn foals can stand, walk, and run within just one hour of birth, allowing them to keep up with the highly mobile herd from an early age. Zebras inhabit a range of habitats across eastern and southern Africa, including open savannas, grasslands, mountainous plateaus, and open woodlands. Many wild zebra populations face serious threats including habitat loss, illegal hunting, competition with livestock, and human-wildlife conflict, leading some species to be classified as vulnerable or endangered. Zebras hold iconic status as symbols of African wildlife, appearing prominently in traditional art, mythology, children’s media, and popular culture across the globe. Their visually stunning appearance, complex social behavior, and adaptability make them extremely popular among wildlife enthusiasts and a flagship species for African conservation efforts.

text:
“I’ll telephone Mark to be at Château Branche with Poppy when we get there, save time going after them,” said Prue, the practical, ringing up the Central as she spoke from the bend in the hall where the telephone table stood, and where she happened to be when Isabel came in.

After this was done, the two little girls sallied forth, Bunkie running ahead and pretending to startle himself with important discoveries along the way. They proceeded to Château Branche by a short cut into the woods.

Mark and Poppy were there waiting for them, thanks to Prue’s foresight, when they reached the great pine in which Mr. Hawthorne had built their house.

“We’ll get right up,” said Prue, beginning to climb the footholds which led into Château Branche.

Isabel handed up the cake to Prue and followed; Mark and Poppy seemed less to climb than to run up, like nuthatches, so agile they both were at this sort of feat.

“Ah!” Mark drew a long breath of delight. “It seems to smell more piney so early in the morning. Isn’t it great to be up in these dark branches?”

“Hark!” whispered Isabel, holding up her hand.

A song so sweet, so liquid, so heart-stirring, that it was like the voice of the woods, of the sky, the green leaves, of June itself, pierced the stillness from a point near at hand.

“Oh, it’s the veery!” whispered Mark, his eyes dilating. He had been taught by his father, wise in woods lore, the note of nearly every bird, and could himself imitate many of them, calling around him the little feathered denizens of the trees.

“It’s a thrush; the veery,” Mark repeated, and the four sat so still that they hardly seemed to breathe, listening to this exquisite song.

At last the veery flew away. The children saw the brown body come out from an oak that stood next to their pine, brighten as it crossed the sunshine, and disappear.

“Why do you sort of want to cry when things are nice that way?” asked Poppy.

“I think because they don’t last,” said Isabel, the poet, who always saw deeper than the others.

text: To scan the lines of his face, or feel the bumps on the head of this Leviathan; this is a thing which no Physiognomist or Phrenologist has as yet undertaken. Such an enterprise would seem almost as hopeful as for Lavater to have scrutinized the wrinkles on the Rock of Gibraltar, or for Gall to have mounted a ladder and manipulated the Dome of the Pantheon. Still, in that famous work of his, Lavater not only treats of the various faces of men, but also attentively studies the faces of horses, birds, serpents, and fish; and dwells in detail upon the modifications of expression discernible therein. Nor have Gall and his disciple Spurzheim failed to throw out some hints touching the phrenological characteristics of other beings than man. Therefore, though I am but ill qualified for a pioneer, in the application of these two semi-sciences to the whale, I will do my endeavor. I try all things; I achieve what I can. Physiognomically regarded, the Sperm Whale is an anomalous creature. He has no proper nose. And since the nose is the central and most conspicuous of the features; and since it perhaps most modifies and finally controls their combined expression; hence it would seem that its entire absence, as an external appendage, must very largely affect the countenance of the whale. For as in landscape gardening, a spire, cupola, monument, or tower of some sort, is deemed almost indispensable to the completion of the scene; so no face can be physiognomically in keeping without the elevated open-work belfry of the nose. Dash the nose from Phidias’s marble Jove, and what a sorry remainder! Nevertheless, Leviathan is of so mighty a magnitude, all his proportions are so stately, that the same deficiency which in the sculptured Jove were hideous, in him is no blemish at all. Nay, it is an added grandeur. A nose to the whale would have been impertinent. As on your physiognomical voyage you sail round his vast head in your jolly-boat, your noble conceptions of him are never insulted by the reflection that he has a nose to be pulled. A pestilent conceit, which so often will insist upon obtruding even when beholding the mightiest royal beadle on his throne.

text: Libraries are iconic quiet public buildings, designed to be sanctuaries for focus and exploration, where the hum of conversation is softened to a whisper. At their core are bright, naturallit reading rooms—spaces where large, unobstructed windows draw in sunlight, casting a warm glow over wooden tables and creating an inviting atmosphere for diving into a novel or poring over a textbook. These rooms are part of libraries’ intentional comfortfocused design, which prioritizes visitor wellbeing: plush soft chairs line corners for casual reading, ergonomic study desks reduce fatigue during long research sessions, and designated quiet zones shield users from distractions—all ensuring that anyone, whether reading for pleasure or working, feels at ease. Beyond reading rooms, libraries are thoughtfully organized with key functional areas. Towering book shelves line walls and aisles, filled with books spanning genres, languages, and eras—from classic literature and academic journals to children’s picture books and local history archives. Complementing these physical collections are modern digital resource hubs, equipped with highspeed internet and access to online databases, ebooks, and digital archives, bridging traditional and contemporary learning tools. Scattered throughout are cozy study corners—some with individual carrels for solo work, others with small tables for group projects—each outfitted with task lighting and power outlets to support productivity. Additionally, dedicated computer access spaces offer free devices and internet, ensuring even those without personal technology can browse the web, complete online forms, or access digital learning materials. Functionally, libraries serve as indispensable information hubs that cater to diverse needs. Students rely on their extensive databases and reference materials to conduct school or university research, while seniors gather for book clubs, storytime sessions, or techhelp workshops that foster connection. Parents bring young children to interactive reading programs, and remote workers use quiet corners as temporary offices. Culturally, libraries are powerful knowledge equality symbols. Unlike spaces where access to information is restricted by cost or status, libraries offer free access to books, resources, and programs to everyone—regardless of age, income, or background—upholding the belief that knowledge is a right, not a privilege. They also stand as lifelong learning encouragers, their designs and offerings adapting across time to inspire continuous growth. This value is evident in both historic and modern libraries: older brickandmortar libraries, with their grand staircases and stainedglass windows, evoke a sense of tradition and reverence for learning, while sleek modern glass libraries, with open layouts and flexible spaces, cater to contemporary needs—yet both prioritize comfort and accessibility. text: Miss Sharp's father was an artist, and had given lessons in drawing at Miss Pinkerton's school. He was a clever man; a pleasant companion; a careless student; with a great propensity for running into debt, and a partiality for the tavern. When he was drunk, he used to beat his wife and daughter; and the next morning, with a headache, he would rail at the world for its neglect of his genius. He was very fond of making fun of his fellow - painters; his jokes were sometimes very smart, it must be confessed, and sometimes not a little broad. He had a great number of debts, in fact, all over the quarter, and lived in a very shabby, poor, dirty house, where he drank, and smoked, and talked to the students of his own class, who used to come in, and hear him holding forth; and who (when they were not smoking his tobacco) used to laugh at him. He had been married to a French opera - girl, who was said to have been a great beauty in her day, but who was now en vieillissant, as the French say, and to have lost all her looks as well as her voice. Miss Sharp always used to declare that her mother was descended from the noble house of d'Aubrion, and spoke of her own fine blood with great pride. Strange, but when this young lady improved in the world, her ancestors improved also. She had heard her mother say, I believe, that the d'Aubrions had once been marquises, but that an elder branch of the family had the title changed into a barony, on the elevation of the Emperor Napoleon. At any rate, Miss Sharp spoke French with a Parisian accent, which was very much in her favour, as we shall hear presently, and obtained the situation of second French mistress in Miss Pinkerton's academy, in consequence of the death of the former incumbent, a lady who was always declaring that she was related to Montmorency and all the most noble families in France, and who could never be got to pronounce a word of French grammar according to the rules laid down by Port - Royal.

text: One night my girlfriend asked what was wrong with me and I couldn’t explain. We lay on my black sheets between my blank white walls, on the bed that was the room’s only furniture. We had bared ourselves — we had a connection when we were naked — but Sandra wanted more than full exposure. It was 3 am after her late shift waiting tables at The Cave, and she smelled like fry oil and strangers, and still she talked. Who was I to prefer silence? I told her how I blacked out as I watched the news, ate my microwave dinner, wrote, how I woke to find my status update a string of *g*’s with no likes, nothing to account for the time between. “It’s not just loneliness, I mean. I’m pretty sure I’m disappearing. People walk straight into me on the street. When I’m alone in a bathroom with 10 urinals, some white guy will come in and pee right next to me.”She twitched her mouth from side to side. This was a habit I envied. She was always doing things equally on either side of her body.When her lips parted the smack echoed off the empty walls.“How long you been feeling this?” she asked. “Like you’re disappearing?”I couldn’t tell whether she was being sarcastic.Well. These were the facts: My cat was dead. My wife and daughter had left me. At some point in the last three years I had stopped going out or having friends. After the divorce I had kept the walls blank because the echo was a kind of company.“Just to clarify,” Sandra said, “you’ve felt like disappearing the whole time you’ve been with me?”“Just to clarify,” I said, “what I mean is you’re all I have left. Maybe you’re the only reason I’m still here.” I felt quite smart about this line.

text: A low murmur pulled him from his thoughts. Near the far wall, a family huddled around a fresh grave. A small coffin, too small for an adult, lay half - covered in dirt. An old man, his back bent with age, looked up and spotted him. The man’s eyes widened, and he stumbled forward, grabbing Padre José’s sleeve. “Father,” he begged, his voice cracking. “It’s my granddaughter. Five years old. She died of fever. Say a prayer. Just one.” Padre José froze. His hands trembled beneath his shabby coat. He had not performed a religious rite in months—not since he’d married his housekeeper to save his own skin, not since he’d started taking the government’s meager pension. To pray now, in front of these people... what if one of them talked? The red shirts paid for information, even from grieving families. “I can’t,” he said, his voice barely audible. The woman beside the grave— the child’s mother—burst into tears. “Please,” she sobbed. “She’s just a little girl. She needs God’s blessing.” The others joined in, their pleas rising like a wail. Padre José felt a sharp twist of shame in his chest. Once, he had been the heart of this community, leading masses, baptizing babies, comforting the dying. Now he stood here, a coward, hiding behind his fear. Temptation gnawed at him— to close his eyes, to recite the words, to feel useful again. But fear rushed back, cold and heavy, like a drug in his veins. “I’m sorry,” he muttered, pulling his arm free. He turned and walked away, his boots crunching on gravel. The sound of their tears followed him, loud and accusing, until he rounded a corner and they faded. He leaned against a tombstone, gasping for breath, and hated himself for his weakness. In a small adobe house across town, Luis’s mother sat on a straw mat, her children clustered around her. She held a tattered book, its pages yellowed and frayed— a forbidden text, full of stories of martyrs. She read aloud about Juan, the young boy who’d died for his faith, her voice soft but steady.

text:
She found her husband in his study. He was sitting at the table, thinking of something. His face looked stern, thoughtful, and guilty. This was not the same Pyotr Dmitritch who had been arguing at dinner and whom his guests knew, but a different man—wearied, feeling guilty and dissatisfied with himself, whom nobody knew but his wife. He must have come to the study to get cigarettes. Before him lay an open cigarette-case full of cigarettes, and one of his hands was in the table drawer; he had paused and sunk into thought as he was taking the cigarettes.

Olga Mihalovna felt sorry for him. It was as clear as day that this man was harassed, could find no rest, and was perhaps struggling with himself. Olga Mihalovna went up to the table in silence: wanting to show that she had forgotten the argument at dinner and was not cross, she shut the cigarette-case and put it in her husband’s coat pocket.

“What should I say to him?” she wondered; “I shall say that lying is like a forest—the further one goes into it the more difficult it is to get out of it. I will say to him, ‘You have been carried away by the false part you are playing; you have insulted people who were attached to you and have done you no harm. Go and apologize to them, laugh at yourself, and you will feel better. And if you want peace and solitude, let us go away together.’”

Meeting his wife’s gaze, Pyotr Dmitritch’s face immediately assumed the expression it had worn at dinner and in the garden—indifferent and slightly ironical. He yawned and got up.

“It’s past five,” he said, looking at his watch. “If our visitors are merciful and leave us at eleven, even then we have another six hours of it. It’s a cheerful prospect, there’s no denying!”

And whistling something, he walked slowly out of the study with his usual dignified gait. She could hear him with dignified firmness cross the dining-room, then the drawing-room, laugh with dignified assurance, and say to the young man who was playing, “Bravo! bravo!” Soon his footsteps died away: he must have gone out into the garden. And now not jealousy, not vexation, but real hatred of his footsteps, his insincere laugh and voice, took possession of Olga Mihalovna. She went to the window and looked out into the garden. Pyotr Dmitritch was already walking along the avenue. Putting one hand in his pocket and snapping the fingers of the other, he walked with confident swinging steps, throwing his head back a little, and looking as though he were very well satisfied with himself, with his dinner, with his digestion, and with nature. . . .

text: The spring sunlight slanted through the tall, leaded windows of the study, gilding the edges of the leather-bound books that lined the walls and turning the scattered sheets of manuscript on the desk to soft gold. Dorothea sat on the wooden chair pulled up to the window, her fingers resting lightly on a page of her late husband Casaubon's unfinished work—his handwriting tight and precise, like he'd been clinging to order even as his health faded. The air smelled of old paper and the faint sweetness of violet blooms from the garden outside, their scent drifting in with the gentle breeze that stirred the curtains. She stared at the words on the page, but her mind kept drifting back to the last months of Casaubon's life—his quiet frustration at his failing research, his fear that his life's work would be forgotten, the way he'd looked at her like she was both his comfort and a reminder of all he couldn't achieve. She'd married him believing she could help him, believing their shared love of knowledge would bind them—but now, with his chair empty and his manuscripts half-finished, she felt a sharp, hollow sense of loss, not just for him, but for the idealistic version of herself she'd left behind. A bird chirped loudly from the maple tree outside, and she looked up, her eyes catching on the garden below—where the grass was bright green and the violets dotted the flower beds like small purple stars. For a second, she let herself imagine a different life: one where she didn't have to live up to someone else's dreams, one where she could chase her own interests, even if they didn't fit the quiet, proper role expected of a widow in Middlemarch. But the thought of her sister Celia's worried face, and the whispers of the townsfolk who'd already judged her for marrying Casaubon in the first place, pulled her back to reality. She closed the manuscript gently, her fingers brushing the edge of the paper, and stood up. The sunlight had shifted, now casting long shadows across the floor, and the violet scent in the air had grown fainter. She walked to the window, pressing her palm against the cool glass, and looked out at the town. In the distance, she could see the spire of the church and the roof of the town hall—familiar sights that had once felt like boundaries, but now felt like parts of a world she might yet learn to navigate on her own terms. She took a deep breath, letting the air fill her lungs, and turned away from the window. The manuscripts were still on the desk, and Casaubon's books still lined the walls—but for the first time since his death, she didn't feel trapped by them. She felt light, almost hopeful, like the breeze that had stirred the curtains earlier, carrying the promise of something new. She picked up one of the manuscript pages, folded it carefully, and slipped it into her pocket— not as a reminder of the past, but as a step toward figuring out what came next.

text: He determined to revisit the scene of the last evening’s gambol, and if he met with any of the party, to demand his dog and gun. As he rose to walk, he found himself stiff in the joints, and wanting in his usual activity. “These mountain beds do not agree with me,” thought Rip, “and if this frolic should lay me up with a fit of the rheumatism, I shall have a blessed time with Dame Van Winkle.” With some difficulty he got down into the glen: he found the gully up which he and his companion had ascended the preceding evening; but to his astonishment a mountain stream was now foaming down it, leaping from rock to rock, and filling the glen with babbling murmurs. He, however, made shift to scramble up its sides, working his toilsome way through thickets of birch, sassafras, and witch-hazel, and sometimes tripped up or entangled by the wild grape-vines that twisted their coils or tendrils from tree to tree, and spread a kind of network in his path. At length he reached to where the ravine had opened through the cliffs to the amphitheatre; but no traces of such opening remained. The rocks presented a high, impenetrable wall, over which the torrent came tumbling in a sheet of feathery foam, and fell into a broad deep basin, black from the shadows of the surrounding forest. Here, then, poor Rip was brought to a stand. He again called and whistled after his dog; he was only answered by the cawing of a flock of idle crows, sporting high in the air about a dry tree that overhung a sunny precipice; and who, secure in their elevation, seemed to look down and scoff at the poor man’s perplexities. What was to be done? the morning was passing away, and Rip felt famished for want of his breakfast. He grieved to give up his dog and gun; he dreaded to meet his wife; but it would not do to starve among the mountains. He shook his head, shouldered the rusty firelock, and, with a heart full of trouble and anxiety, turned his steps homeward. As he approached the village he met a number of people, but none whom he knew, which somewhat surprised him, for he had thought himself acquainted with every one in the country round. Their dress, too, was of a different fashion from that to which he was accustomed. They all stared at him with equal marks of surprise, and whenever they cast their eyes upon him, invariably stroked their chins. The constant recurrence of this gesture induced Rip, involuntarily, to do the same, when, to his astonishment, he found his beard had grown a foot long!

text:
I stood dumb. Surely it was fortunate that I had discarded the old motor-coat for that ordinary overcoat I had bought in the London Road. Nevertheless, I realized that I should never be able to go forth in the daylight, lest I might be recognized.

Therefore, I prepared myself to settle down to a dull, uneventful life, hourly fearing that my somewhat inquisitive landlady might read in her newspaper the description of me which had been circulated, and thus identify me with the man of whom the police were in such active search. What then?

Next morning I received a surprise; for, on being ushered into the back room for breakfast, I found that I had as fellow-lodger a slim, good-looking girl, with soft brown eyes and wavy auburn hair. She was already at table reading the newspaper when Mrs. Bowyer introduced her as Miss Lisely Hatten.

I look back upon it all now. Was she to be an instrument of Fate?

When I sat down with her and we began to chat, I learned that she was a typist, employed in a great insurance office in Cornhill. She was quietly but smartly dressed, with neat stockings and shoes, and I confess I rather liked her from the first.

I explained that I was a journalist and worked at home most part of the day, when suddenly she caused me to start by glancing at the paper and remarking:

“That’s a very mysterious affair, the murder in the street in Bloomsbury Square! Have you seen it? What do you think of it?”

I inhaled a deep breath.

“Oh! I suppose it was a crime of jealousy. Don’t you think so? One sees such scenes in the pictures.”

“I don’t know,” she replied very seriously. “I’d like to see the murderer arrested. Poor girl! If I were in her place, I’d hunt the devil down to the bitter end. Why should he shoot her lover in cold blood—go up and kill him without warning? The poor man had no chance of self-defence. It was done by some young bounder about town—some lounge-lizard or good-looking dancing-partner, perhaps.”

“Possibly,” I agreed, thankful that the suspicions of the good-looking young business girl had not been aroused by the description of myself which was being everywhere circulated.

text: As she closed her eyes, she heard a noise outside the dungeon door. It creaked open, and a figure slipped in. It was Aline. She was carrying a lantern, and in her hand she held a loaf of bread and a knife. “Quick,” she whispered. “You must escape. My father is going to burn you tomorrow.” Ursula stared at her in surprise. “Why are you helping me?” she asked. “Because I cannot bear to see anyone suffer,” Aline replied. “My parents are wrong to be so cruel. I do not believe in burning people for their faith.” She cut the ropes that bound Ursula’s wrists, and handed her the bread. “There is a small door at the back of the hall,” she said. “It leads to the woods. You must run as fast as you can, and never look back.” Ursula took the bread, but she did not move. “What about Robert?” she said. “He must come too.” Aline shook her head. “I cannot free him,” she said. “The door to his cell is locked with a big key, and my father keeps it with him. But I have left a note for his friends, telling them when he will be taken to York. They will rescue him.” Ursula hesitated for a moment. Then she turned to Aline. “Thank you,” she said, in a voice that was almost kind. She ran to the small door that Aline had told her about. As she opened it, she looked back at the hall. She could see the lights in the windows, and she could hear Lady Eleanor’s cold voice shouting orders. She gritted her teeth, and ran into the woods. The moon was shining, and it lit up her path. She ran as fast as she could, her feet crunching on the frozen leaves. She did not stop until she was far away from Holwick Hall. When she finally collapsed on the ground, exhausted, she knew that her life would never be the same again. She was free, but her hatred still burned inside her. She would never forget Holwick Hall, or the people who had made her life a misery. And one day, she would return.

text: Among the lizards, a gecko has been mentioned as a light-giver, as if these curious creatures were not remarkable enough in themselves without this attendant phenomenon. According to Dr. Carpenter, the eggs of the gray lizard have been seen to emit light; and in Surinam he states that a frog or toad is luminous, especially in the interior of its mouth. Thus we see that this strange light is found in some form from the lowest to the highest animals,—one of the commonest of phenomena, yet presenting a problem defying solution. Dr. Phipson, the eminent scientist, states that he once observed certain phenomena in man, the light being a brilliant scintillation of a metallic pink color. It is well known that human beings under certain physical conditions become luminous. In some cases among the ignorant great excitement has been occasioned, and the victim avoided as a pest, or something capable of dire disaster to the entire community. In a small German village, an English physician discovered a man who was luminous at night, and who had caused much alarm among the superstitious. Bartholin records an instance of an Italian lady whom he calls Mulier splendens, who suddenly found that, when rubbed with a linen cloth in the dark, her body gave out a brilliant phosphorescent light; so that she appeared in a darkened room like a veritable fire-body, an awe-striking object to her superstitious servant, who fled from her speechless with fear and amazement, thinking that her mistress was being consumed. Dr. Kane records a very curious instance of luminosity, probably electric, which played about his person. He was on[117] his way with Petersen to an Esquimau settlement, in order to procure food. Their thermometer indicated -42° C. (-44° Fahr.). With their weary dogs and sledges, they had reached some untenanted huts at a place called Anoatok, after thirty miles march from the ship. "We took to the best hut," says Dr. Kane, "filled in its broken front with snow, housed our dogs, and crawled in among them. It was too cold to sleep. Next morning we broke down our door, and tried the dogs again. They could hardly stand. A gale now set in from the south-west, obscuring the moon, and blowing very hard. We were forced back into the hut; but after corking up all the openings with snow, and making a fire with our Esquimau lamp, we got up the temperature to 30° below zero, Fahr., cooked coffee, and fed the dogs freely. This done, Petersen and myself, our clothing frozen stiff, fell asleep through pure exhaustion; the wind outside blowing death to all that might be exposed to its influence.

text: The line rose slowly and steadily, then the surface of the ocean bulged ahead of the boat and the fish came out. He came out unendingly, water pouring from his sides. He was bright in the sun—his head and back were dark purple, and in the sun the stripes on his sides showed wide and a light lavender. His sword was as long as a baseball bat, tapered like a rapier; he rose his full length from the water, then re-entered it smoothly, like a diver. The old man saw the great scythe-blade of his tail go under, and the line commenced to race out. "He is two feet longer than the skiff," the old man said. The line was going out fast but steadily, and the fish was not panicked. The old man tried with both hands to keep the line just inside breaking strength. He knew that if he could not slow the fish with steady pressure, the fish would take out all the line and break it. He is a great fish, and I must convince him, he thought. I must never let him learn his strength, nor what he could do if he made his run. If I were him, I would put in everything now and go until something broke. But thank God, they are not as intelligent as we who kill them—though they are more noble, more able. The old man had seen many great fish. He had seen many that weighed more than a thousand pounds, and he had caught two of that size in his life—but never alone. Now, alone and out of sight of land, he was fast to the biggest fish he had ever seen, bigger than he had ever heard of. His left hand was still as tight as the gripped claws of an eagle. It will uncramp, though, he thought. Surely it will uncramp to help my right hand. There are three things that are brothers: the fish, and my two hands. It must uncramp. It is unworthy of it to be cramped.

text: Riverside High’s annual “Future Tech Forum” featured a heated debate: “Should AI Make Decisions for Humans in Education and Healthcare?” Organized by the school’s tech club, the event brought together 12 students— six arguing “Pro” and six “Con”— and a panel of teachers and local tech experts as judges. “This isn’t just about AI— it’s about what it means to be human,” tech club advisor Mr. Hayes said in his opening speech. “Argue with facts, listen with an open mind, and remember: progress needs balance.” The Pro team, led by 11th-grader Eli, kicked off with education examples. “AI tutors can adapt to students’ learning paces— a student struggling with math gets extra practice, while an advanced learner moves faster,” Eli explained, citing a study where AI tutoring improved test scores by 23%. “It’s not replacing teachers— it’s giving them tools to help every student succeed.” His teammate Lila added a healthcare angle: “AI can analyze medical scans faster than humans, catching diseases like cancer in early stages when treatment is most effective.” The Con team, led by Mia, pushed back with ethical concerns. “AI learns from data— if the data has biases, the decisions will too,” Mia argued, referencing a case where an AI college admissions tool favored wealthy students. “Education is about more than test scores— a teacher notices when a student is stressed or lonely, but AI can’t read emotions.” On healthcare, her teammate Jamal noted: “Patients need human empathy. Imagine hearing you have an illness from a machine instead of a doctor who can answer your fears.” The debate intensified as students questioned each other’s sources. “Your AI tutoring study only looked at short-term scores— what about long-term creativity?” Mia asked Eli. Eli responded: “AI frees up time for teachers to focus on creativity, like group projects or art.” When Jamal brought up bias, Lila countered: “Engineers are working on ‘fair AI’— we just need better regulations, not to reject the technology.” After the final arguments, the judges praised both teams for their depth. “You didn’t just take sides— you explored the gray areas,” said judge Dr. Chen, a local AI researcher. The audience voted, and the Con team won by a narrow margin, but Mr. Hayes emphasized: “This isn’t a win-lose— it’s a starting point for thinking critically about tech.” Later, Eli and Mia chatted by the forum’s snack table. “I still think AI has huge potential,” Eli said. Mia nodded: “Me too— but only if we keep humans in charge. Tech should serve us, not the other way around.” For the Riverside High students, the debate wasn’t just a competition. It was a lesson that innovation without ethics is risky, that listening to different perspectives strengthens arguments, and that the future of tech depends on balancing progress with the values that make us human.

Yergunov looked to see which was the biggest, swung his whip and lashed at it with all his might. A small, long-legged puppy turned its sharp muzzle upwards and set up a shrill, piercing howl.

Yergunov stood for a long while at the window, tapping. But at last the hoar-frost on the trees near the house glowed red, and a muffled female figure appeared with a lantern in her hands.

text: The autumn dawn spread pale light over the Clutter farm, turning the dry cornfields around the house a dull gold. Alvin Dewey stood at the edge of the dirt driveway, his hands in the pockets of his heavy overcoat, and stared at the wooden farmhouse—its windows dark, its porch steps swept clean, like nothing terrible had ever happened there. The air smelled of turned earth from the plowed fields and the faint, sharp scent of diesel from the sheriff's car parked beside him, mixing with the cold mist that clung to his boots. He paused, pulling a notebook from his coat, and flipped to the page with the crime scene notes: four dead, no forced entry, a missing radio and a few dollars from the safe. He'd been working the case for three days, interviewing neighbors, tracing the Clutters' last hours, but every lead felt like a dead end. The town of Holcomb was quiet, too quiet—people locked their doors, avoided talking about the murders, like silence could keep the evil away. A crow cawed from a bare tree, and Dewey looked up, squinting at the sky. It was going to be a clear day, no clouds, no rain—nothing to wash away the traces of what had happened. He thought of Herb Clutter, the farmer who'd been known for his kindness, for lending tools to neighbors, for never turning away a stranger. And now he was gone, along with his wife and two of their children, killed for no reason anyone could see. He walked toward the cornfield, his boots crunching on the dry stalks. The rows stretched on, endless, until they faded into the distance. He imagined the killers walking through here, hiding, watching the house. What had they been thinking? Did they feel anything—fear, guilt, even a spark of regret? Or were they just empty, just machines that killed and moved on? The mist lifted, and the sun broke through, warming his face. He pulled out a cigarette, lighting it slowly, and took a long drag. The smoke stung his throat, but it helped—helped him focus, helped him push down the anger and the sadness that threatened to overwhelm him. He had a job to do: find the men who did this, make them answer for it. For the Clutters, for the town, for himself.

text:
“You are crazy. . . .”
The two men looked at each other, probably because the same thought—of the boundless plains, the unending forests and swamps—struck both of them at once.
“Well, I see you have gone off your head,” the jeune premier commented. “I’ll tell you what, old man. . . . First thing, go to bed, then drink some brandy and tea to put you into a sweat. And some castor-oil, of course. Stay, where am I to get some brandy?”
Brama-Glinsky thought a minute, then made up his mind to go to a shopkeeper called Madame Tsitrinnikov to try and get it from her on tick: who knows? perhaps the woman would feel for them and let them have it. The jeune premier went off, and half an hour later returned with a bottle of brandy and some castor-oil. Shtchiptsov was sitting motionless, as before, on the bed, gazing dumbly at the floor. He drank the castor-oil offered him by his friend like an automaton, with no consciousness of what he was doing. Like an automaton he sat afterwards at the table, and drank tea and brandy; mechanically he emptied the whole bottle and let the jeune premier put him to bed. The latter covered him up with a quilt and an overcoat, advised him to get into a perspiration, and went away.
The night came on; Shtchiptsov had drunk a great deal of brandy, but he did not sleep. He lay motionless under the quilt and stared at the dark ceiling; then, seeing the moon looking in at the window, he turned his eyes from the ceiling towards the companion of the earth, and lay so with open eyes till the morning. At nine o’clock in the morning Zhukov, the manager, ran in.
“What has put it into your head to be ill, my angel?” he cackled, wrinkling up his nose. “Aie, aie! A man with your physique has no business to be ill! For shame, for shame! Do you know, I was quite frightened. ‘Can our conversation have had such an effect on him?’ I wondered. My dear soul, I hope it’s not through me you’ve fallen ill! You know you gave me as good . . . er . . . And, besides, comrades can never get on without words. You called me all sorts of names . . . and have gone at me with your fists too, and yet I am fond of you! Upon my soul, I am. I respect you and am fond of you! Explain, my angel, why I am so fond of you. You are neither kith nor kin nor wife, but as soon as I heard you had fallen ill it cut me to the heart.”

text: A teacher is a dedicated, compassionate professional who plays a vital role in shaping the minds, character, and future of students, guiding them through their educational journey from early childhood to adulthood. More than just instructors who impart knowledge, teachers are mentors, role models, and supporters, helping students develop critical thinking skills, emotional intelligence, and a lifelong love of learning. Teachers work in a variety of settings, including preschools, elementary schools, middle schools, high schools, colleges, and universities, as well as online learning platforms, catering to students of all ages and backgrounds. Their responsibilities extend far beyond lesson planning and classroom instruction: they prepare lesson plans that align with curriculum standards, deliver engaging, interactive lessons that cater to different learning styles (visual, auditory, kinesthetic), assess student progress through tests, quizzes, and assignments, and provide feedback to help students improve. Teachers also create a safe, inclusive classroom environment where all students feel valued, respected, and supported, regardless of their abilities, background, or learning needs. They address behavioral issues, resolve conflicts between students, and provide emotional support to students who may be facing personal challenges, such as family problems, anxiety, or low self-esteem. Many teachers work extra hours outside of class, grading papers, preparing materials, meeting with parents or guardians to discuss student progress, and participating in professional development workshops to enhance their teaching skills. To become a teacher, individuals typically need a bachelor’s degree in education or a specific subject area, as well as a teaching license or certification, which requires completing student teaching internships and passing exams. Some teachers pursue advanced degrees, such as a master’s or doctoral degree, to specialize in areas like special education, curriculum design, or educational administration. Teachers must possess a range of skills, including strong communication skills to effectively convey information to students and collaborate with colleagues, patience to work with students of different abilities and learning paces, creativity to design engaging lessons, and adaptability to adjust their teaching methods to meet the needs of individual students. They also need to be organized to manage classroom activities, track student progress, and meet deadlines for grading and lesson planning. The impact of a teacher extends far beyond the classroom: a good teacher can inspire students to pursue their dreams, build their confidence, and develop the skills they need to succeed in life. They help students develop important life skills, such as responsibility, teamwork, and problem-solving, and instill values like honesty, respect, and empathy. Despite the challenges of the profession—including long hours, heavy workloads, and emotional demands—many teachers find great fulfillment in seeing their students grow, learn, and achieve their goals. Teachers are essential to society, as they prepare the next generation of leaders, professionals, and citizens, ensuring that society continues to grow and thrive. Whether teaching young children to read and write, guiding high school students through complex subjects, or mentoring college students as they prepare for their careers, teachers play an irreplaceable role in shaping the future of our world.

text:
The second day began like the first. The housekeeper rose before dawn and although there was not a smudge of dirt or a speck of dust anywhere in the house, she washed and swept and rubbed and polished as before. Then she hurried to the market early to buy a new spray of flowers. The artist got up early, too, and made himself as worthy as possible of reflecting upon the Buddha. And once more when he went to pray, there was Good Fortune, shining like a narcissus, and gold as a narcissus' heart, and black as a beetle on a narcissus petal, sitting quietly before the shelf where sat the household image of the Buddha. No sooner did she see the artist than she jumped to her feet, lowered her head as though she were bowing, and moved over to make room for him. They meditated as before, the artist occasionally striking his hands softly, and the cat sitting very still and proper with her paws side by side.

Then the artist went into his room beside the hydrangeas. To-day he reflected upon the renunciation of Siddhartha. Again he was the prince, but now he ordered his chariot and for the first time drove unannounced through the city. He saw an old man, and a man sick with fever, and a dead man. He looked at his bracelets—but gold could do no good to such as these. He, the prince of the land, was at last helpless to help.

The head of the artist hung heavy on his breast. He thought he smelled a garland of flowers but the sweetness sickened him. They brought word that a son had been born to him, but he only thought how sad life would be for the child. When the housekeeper came with rice, he sent her away without tasting it, and when Good Fortune wandered in with big watchful eyes, he told her that he was in no mood for entertainment. Evening drew closer but still the artist did not stir. The housekeeper looked in but went away again. Good Fortune mewed anxiously, but the artist did not hear her.

For now the artist imagined that Prince Siddhartha had secretly sent for his chariot driver and Kanthaka, his white horse. He had gazed long at his sleeping wife and the little baby she held in her arms. Now he was in the darkness of his garden; now he rode quietly through the sleeping city;

We said good - bye, and Dill went inside the house. He evidently remembered he was engaged to me, for he ran back out and kissed me swiftly in front of Jem. "Yawl write, hear?" he bawled after us. Every night - sound I heard from my cot on the back porch was magnified three - fold; every scratch of feet on gravel was Boo Radley seeking revenge, every passing Negro laughing in the night was Boo Radley coming for us. The full meaning of the night's events hit me and I began to cry. Jem held me in his arms and tried to comfort me. "It's all right, Scout," he said. "Don't be scared. Boo Radley didn't hurt us." "But he could have," I said. "He could have killed you." Jem was silent for a moment. Then he said, "I don't think he wanted to hurt us, Scout. He—he was just trying to get us out of the way." "How do you know?" I asked. "Because—because when he passed by me, he didn't even look at me. He just went on by. text: All this happened, more or less. The war parts, anyway, are pretty much true. One guy I knew really was shot in Dresden for taking a teapot that wasn't his. Another guy I knew really did threaten to have his personal enemies killed by hired gunmen after the war. And so on. I've changed all the names. I really did go back to Dresden with Guggenheim money. It was a very good thing for me to do, and I was able to finish this book at last. One time I had to call in a couple of favors to get a friend out of a Russian zone in Germany. He was a private, and he was being held as a spy. I went to the Russian zone in a rented car with the friend's wife. The Russians had a wall around the zone, and they had a gate in the wall. The gate was a rainbow of rusty iron. I had to talk to a Russian officer who was a tanker. He had a chest full of medals. He was a very short man, and he was in a very bad mood. He said we couldn't have the private. He was extremely surly. He had a little mustache. I asked him if the war was over for him. He said, 'How do you mean?' I said, 'The war is over for me. I don't have to fight anymore. I can be polite now.' He said, 'It is over when I say it is over.' So I said, 'You must be a very important man.' He said, 'I am the commandant here.' So I said, 'I am a very important man in America. I would be grateful if you would call my friend in Moscow. He will tell you to let the private go.' The commandant said, 'You have a friend in Moscow?' I said, 'Yes. He is a famous writer.' The commandant said, 'What is his name?' I told him. He had never heard of the writer. So I said, 'I will write a book about this someday.' He said, 'You do that.' So the private stayed in the Russian zone. On the way back, the private's wife cried. “Panteley!” called Yegorushka.

No answer followed. But now a gust of wind for the last time flung up the mat and hurried away. A quiet regular sound was heard. A big cold drop fell on Yegorushka’s knee, another trickled over his hand. He noticed that his knees were not covered, and tried to rearrange the mat, but at that moment something began pattering on the road, then on the shafts and the bales. It was the rain. As though they understood one another, the rain and the mat began prattling of something rapidly, gaily and most annoyingly like two magpies.

Yegorushka knelt up or rather squatted on his boots. While the rain was pattering on the mat, he leaned forward to screen his knees, which were suddenly wet. He succeeded in covering his knees, but in less than a minute was aware of a penetrating, unpleasant dampness behind on his back and the calves of his legs. He returned to his former position, exposing his knees to the rain, and wondered what to do to rearrange the mat which he could not see in the darkness. But his arms were already wet, the water was trickling up his sleeves and down his collar, and his shoulder-blades felt chilly. And he made up his mind to do nothing but sit motionless and wait till it was all over.

“Holy, holy, holy!” he whispered.

Suddenly, exactly over his head, the sky cracked with a fearful deafening din; he huddled up and held his breath, waiting for the fragments to fall upon his head and back. He inadvertently opened his eyes and saw a blinding intense light flare out and flash five times on his fingers, his wet sleeves, and on the trickles of water running from the mat upon the bales and down to the ground. There was a fresh peal of thunder as violent and awful; the sky was not growling and rumbling now, but uttering short crashing sounds like the crackling of dry wood.

He ran to the craft bin and grabbed a small box. “Let’s put the flowers in here!” he said, handing the box to Tom. Tom tucked the flowers inside, and they stayed tidy. “Gus, you’re smart!” Lily said. By Friday, the game was ready. On fair day, their booth was busy. Gus gave each kid a blindfold and spun them gently. “Walk straight— almost there!” he said, guiding a little girl. Lily helped her pick a flower sticker, and Tom clapped when she pinned it close to the garden. “You did great!” he said. A boy wanted to pin a flower, but he was scared of the blindfold. “It’s okay— I’ll hold your hand,” Gus said softly. Lily showed him the game board: “See? The garden is friendly!” The boy nodded, and with Gus’s help, he pinned his flower perfectly. “Yay!” he shouted. At the end of the fair, Ms. Bell brought a trophy to their booth. “Your team worked so well together— everyone did their part!” she said. Lily, Tom, and Gus hugged each other. “We didn’t do it alone,” Lily said. “Tom cut the flowers, Gus helped the kids, and we fixed the mess together!” That night, Gus told his mom about the fair. “Working with friends is fun!” he said. For the three friends, the spring fair wasn’t just a game. It was a lesson that when everyone helps each other, they can make something wonderful— and have a lot of fun along the way.

text: The summer night hung hot and still over Maycomb, with the smell of pine from the woods on the edge of town drifting toward the jail. Scout Finch walked beside Atticus, her hand in his, her bare feet kicking up dust from the dirt road—she'd snuck out of the house after dinner, following Jem and Dill, and now here she was, standing in the shadow of the jail, watching a group of men in overalls cluster around her father. The air smelled of sweat and whiskey from the men, mixing with the faint, sweet scent of jasmine from a bush by the jail door. She paused, squeezing Atticus's hand tighter, and stared at the men's faces—hard, angry faces, the kind she'd never seen on the usual folks at the general store. One of them stepped forward, his voice low: 'You gonna move, Finch?' Atticus didn't flinch. 'I'm not moving,' he said. Scout's throat felt tight. She didn't understand why these men were mad, why they were yelling about Tom Robinson, why Atticus looked like he was waiting for something to break. Then she saw Mr. Cunningham, standing at the back of the group—his overalls were too big, his hat pulled low, the same Mr. Cunningham who'd borrowed turnips from her father last winter, who'd paid back with a sack of nuts. She took a step forward, forgetting to be scared. 'Mr. Cunningham?' she said. 'How's your boy Walter? He didn't come to school today—Jem and I were gonna walk with him tomorrow.' The men went quiet. Mr. Cunningham stared at her, his face softening. He nodded, slow, then turned to the others. 'Let's go,' he said. One by one, the men walked away, their boots scraping the dirt. Scout looked up at Atticus—his eyes were shiny, like he was gonna cry. 'You okay?' she asked. He knelt down, squeezing her shoulders. 'I'm fine, Scout,' he said. 'You're the one who's okay.' They walked back home, the jail's iron bars fading behind them. The town was quiet now, most of the houses dark, except for Miss Maudie's—her porch light was on, like she was waiting. Scout thought about Mr. Cunningham, about the way his face changed when she talked about Walter, about how angry men could turn quiet just because a kid said hello. She thought about Tom Robinson, locked up in that jail, and wondered if he knew someone was trying to help him. Atticus tucked her into bed that night, sitting on the edge of the mattress. 'You know why you shouldn't kill a mockingbird, Scout?' he said. She nodded. ''Cause they don't do nothin' but sing.' Atticus smiled.

text: Second: To the native Indian of Peru, the continual sight of the snow-howdahed Andes conveys naught of dread, except, perhaps, in the mere fancying of the eternal frosted desolateness reigning at such vast altitudes, and the natural conceit of what a fearfulness it would be to lose oneself in such inhuman solitudes. Not so the sailor, beholding the scenery of the Antarctic seas; where at times, by some infernal trick of legerdemain in the powers of frost and air, he, shivering and half shipwrecked, instead of rainbows speaking hope and solace to his misery, views what seems a boundless churchyard grinning upon him with its lean ice monuments and splintered crosses. Tell me, why this strong young colt, foaled in some peaceful valley of Vermont, far removed from all beasts of prey—why is it that upon the sunniest day, if you but shake a fresh buffalo robe behind him, so that he cannot even see it, but only smells its wild animal muskiness—why will he start, snort, and with bursting eyes paw the ground in phrensies of affright? There is no remembrance in him of any gorings of wild creatures in his green northern home, so that the strange muskiness he smells cannot recall to him anything associated with the experience of former perils; for what knows he, this New England colt, of the black bisons of distant Oregon? text: Moroccan tagine is a beloved slowcooked stew, inseparable from the conical clay pot also called a tagine that gives it its name—this unique vessel is key to the dish’s signature texture and flavor. At its heart is tender meat, typically lamb for rich, gamey depth or chicken for milder succulence, which develops a rich deep brown color after browning, thanks to a rub of warm spices like paprika and cinnamon. It’s paired with a vibrant mix of ingredients: sweet dried fruits plump prunes, chewy apricots, or even dates, which caramelize slightly during cooking and earthy vegetables orange carrots, creamy potatoes, or tender turnips, all simmered together in a thick, aromatic sauce that clings to every bite. The tagine pot’s magic lies in its design: the conical lid traps steam, creating a moist cooking environment that keeps the meat and vegetables incredibly moist—no dry, tough bites here. As it cooks, gentle steam escapes through the lid’s small top vent, while the sauce reduces slowly, concentrating flavors and developing a glossy sheen that makes it look glistening when ladled into bowls. Tastewise, tagine is a masterclass in balancing sweet and savory: the tender meat melts in your mouth, infused with the sauce’s depth; dried fruits add a natural sweetness that cuts through the meat’s richness; salty spices cumin, coriander, and a pinch of salt ground the dish; and a subtle smoky note from smoked paprika adds layers of complexity. The sauce itself is deeply aromatic, with hints of saffron for luxury or ginger for brightness, making every spoonful feel both comforting and exotic. Culturally, tagine is the centerpiece of Moroccan hospitality. It’s slowcooked for hours, often prepared for family meals, holiday feasts, or to welcome guests—served alongside fluffy couscous which soaks up every drop of the thick sauce or warm flatbread. Sharing a tagine is a ritual of connection, with the dish’s hearty, layered flavors reflecting Moroccan culinary traditions of blending sweet and savory. Its preparation relies on intentional, unrushed steps—slowcooking is nonnegotiable for depth: 1. Browning: The meat is seasoned with spices, then seared in the tagine pot or a heavybottomed pan until it develops a deep brown crust. This step seals in juices and adds a nutty, caramelized flavor that forms the base of the stew. 2. Infusing: Aromatics like onions, garlic, and spices cumin, coriander, paprika are sautéed in the same pot, releasing their fragrances to infuse the oil. This “spice base” ensures every ingredient in the tagine absorbs those warm, aromatic notes. 3. Simmering: The browned meat, dried fruits, and vegetables are added to the pot, along with broth or water. The tagine is covered, and the stew simmers gently over low heat for 23 hours or longer for lamb. The conical lid traps steam, tenderizing the meat and letting the sauce thicken and deepen in flavor—no stirring needed, just patience. This slowcooking process transforms simple ingredients into a dish that’s as rich in flavor as it is in cultural significance, making tagine a timeless favorite around the world..

text: It is not the least among the strange things bred by the intense artificialness of sea-usages, that while in the open air of the deck some officers will, upon provocation, bear themselves boldly and defyingly enough towards their commander; yet, ten to one, let those very officers the next moment go down to their customary dinner in that same commander’s cabin, and straightway their inoffensive, not to say deprecatory and humble air towards him, as he sits at the head of the table; this is marvellous, sometimes most comical. Now, if to this consideration you superadd the official supremacy of a ship-master, then, by inference, you will derive the cause of that peculiarity of sea-life just mentioned. Over his ivory-inlaid table, Ahab presided like a mute, maned sea-lion on the white coral beach, surrounded by his warlike but still deferential cubs. In his own proper turn, each officer waited to be served. They were as little children before Ahab; and yet, in Ahab, there seemed not to lurk the smallest social arrogance. With one mind, their intent eyes all fastened upon the old man’s knife, as he carved the chief dish before him. I do not suppose that for the world they would have profaned that moment with the slightest observation, even upon so neutral a topic as the weather. No! text:
The long and narrow peninsula of Malacca, extending south-eastward from the territories of Birmah, forms the most southerly point of all Asia. In a continuous line from that peninsula stretch the long islands of Sumatra, Java, Bally, and Timor; which, with many others, form a vast mole, or rampart, lengthwise connecting Asia with Australia, and dividing the long unbroken Indian ocean from the thickly studded oriental archipelagoes. This rampart is pierced by several sally-ports for the convenience of ships and whales; conspicuous among which are the straits of Sunda and Malacca. By the straits of Sunda, chiefly, vessels bound to China from the west, emerge into the China seas.
Those narrow straits of Sunda divide Sumatra from Java; and standing midway in that vast rampart of islands, buttressed by that bold green promontory, known to seamen as Java Head; they not a little correspond to the central gateway opening into some vast walled empire: and considering the inexhaustible wealth of spices, and silks, and jewels, and gold, and ivory, with which the thousand islands of that oriental sea are enriched, it seems a significant provision of nature, that such treasures, by the very formation of the land, should at least bear the appearance, however ineffectual, of being guarded from the all-grasping western world. The shores of the Straits of Sunda are unsupplied with those domineering fortresses which guard the entrances to the Mediterranean, the Baltic, and the Propontis. Unlike the Danes, these Orientals do not demand the obsequious homage of lowered top-sails from the endless procession of ships before the wind, which for centuries past, by night and by day, have passed between the islands of Sumatra and Java, freighted with the costliest cargoes of the east. But while they freely waive a ceremonial like this, they do by no means renounce their claim to more solid tribute.
